case_study_insert.main_stem: Southswell Surf School (SWS) is a sole trader in the surf school and beach resort sector, employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2014 by Riley Tanaka, the business runs lessons, board hire and a small beach café at Flagstaff Beach, with a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership. SWS plans to invest $340,000 in a new beachfront learn-to-surf centre with solar showers and a board repair workshop, financed by a $200,000 ten-year bank loan and a $140,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $52,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $22, and currently produces 9,600 units a year. SWS faces two operational problems: labour turnover among instructors has reached 22% and complaints about lesson safety briefings are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Summer 2025: A survey of 450 beach visitors found that 58% would book a five-day group lesson package, and the average lesson rating on review sites is 4.6 out of 5. Customer complaints fell from 19 to 8 per month, and average board-repair turnaround is 2.5 days. Of 24 employees, 9 do not hold a current off-the-job water-safety instructor certificate; courses at the coastal college cost $600 per employee. Peak-season occupancy on the beach reached 84% across 13 weekend sessions.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Southswell Surf School as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing overdraft and variable-loan costs for small businesses. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.40 to $12.07 per hour from April 2026, raising seasonal instructor wage bills. (3) Wetsuit neoprene and repair-foam input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, leisure inflation is running at 6.9%, and consumer spending on coastal leisure grew 5.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: SWS plans to finance its new learn-to-surf centre with a bank loan rather than extending its overdraft. Explain two advantages for SWS of using a $200,000 ten-year bank loan instead of a $140,000 overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A ten-year bank loan gives SWS a known, fixed repayment schedule, which makes budgeting and break-even planning far easier than an overdraft that can be withdrawn or repriced at short notice. With fixed costs of $52,000 a year and $22 prices, Riley Tanaka can forecast monthly repayments against 9,600 units of annual lesson output and avoid being caught short during quiet winter weeks.

Point 2: The bank loan is designed for long-term investment, so the $200,000 is cheaper and more stable than rolling an overdraft indefinitely; overdraft interest is typically higher and unsecured limits are reviewed frequently. Using the loan for the $340,000 centre also frees the overdraft for genuine working-capital swings, such as buying wetsuits before the 5.4% rise in coastal leisure demand, and reduces the risk of the bank cancelling short-term funding mid-expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Southswell Surf School and its learn-to-surf centre decision.

questions.question_text: SWS is launching its new beachfront learn-to-surf centre. Consider roadside billboard advertising along the coastal highway, partnerships with beach hotels and holiday parks, or social media partnerships with surf influencers. Which should SWS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Roadside billboard advertising: A run of billboards along the coastal highway would reach holiday traffic driving to Flagstaff Beach during the season, building strong local awareness cheaply. However, most drivers are passing through rather than booking lessons, conversion is hard to measure, and reach collapses in winter, so the spend could be wasted on non-buyers for a 24-employee sole trader funding a $340,000 centre.

Beach hotel and holiday-park partnerships: Formal referral agreements with nearby hotels and parks would place SWS directly in front of families already planning beach holidays, matching the 58% of 450 surveyed visitors who said they would book a five-day group lesson package. Commissions of 10–15% per booking add cost, and partners may promote competitors, but this channel delivers ready-made groups with zero media spend.

Surf influencer partnerships: Paying credible surf influencers to feature the new centre and its solar showers builds national awareness, suits the visual nature of the product, and can be tracked through discount codes. Costs are flexible and engagement measurable, though results build slowly and depend on the influencer's authenticity with a safety-conscious audience.

Recommendation: SWS should choose beach hotel and holiday-park partnerships. They convert warm holiday demand into confirmed group bookings at low fixed cost, reinforce the 4.6 out of 5 rating and the 58% booking intent found in its research, and keep SWS in control of the safety message. Highway billboards are rejected as untrackable and seasonal with wastage among passing traffic; influencer campaigns are rejected as too slow to fill the 84% peak-season occupancy target, and can be layered in later as a secondary channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SWS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SWS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SWS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why billboards and influencer marketing are rejected as the primary channel.

questions.question_text: SWS's labour turnover among instructors has reached 22%. Explain two benefits for SWS of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation among its experienced surf instructors.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives SWS's experienced instructors the freedom to design their own lesson sequences, spot corrections and safety drills, satisfying their need for autonomy and professional trust (Herzberg's motivator factors). Instructors who feel ownership of their coaching are more likely to stay, directly tackling the 22% turnover and protecting the 4.6 out of 5 average lesson rating that wins repeat bookings.

Point 2: Empowered instructors respond faster to real beach conditions than centralised instruction would allow — tide, wind and crowd changes require judgement that cannot be micromanaged from the café. This improves lesson safety and quality, cutting complaints further from their fall to 8 per month, and reduces the need to recruit and recertify replacements, saving the $600 per employee off-the-job water-safety cost for the 9 staff who still need certification.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SWS's labour turnover, safety image and certification gap.

questions.question_text: SWS needs certified water-safety coverage for its new learn-to-surf centre. Consider recruiting additional fully certified instructors externally, or upskilling existing staff through the $600 coastal-college certificate. Which should SWS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment of certified instructors: Hiring already-certificated instructors fills the safety gap immediately, brings fresh techniques and can add capacity for the new centre from day one, which suits the 84% peak-season occupancy. However, certified coastal instructors are scarce and command premium wages, recruitment fees add cost, and new hires do not yet know SWS's lesson protocols, so safety-briefing quality could vary while they settle in.

Upskilling existing staff: Certifying the 9 unqualified staff at $600 each costs $5,400 in total and keeps continuity of SWS's own lesson method and safety culture. Staff develop loyalty, retention improves, and the school keeps its 24-strong team intact, but the course must be completed before they can lead sessions alone, creating short-term cover problems, and two staff could pass the course but still lack judgement in rough water.

Decision: SWS should upskill the 9 existing staff, hiring at most one external senior instructor as a mentor and safety lead. Upskilling costs $5,400 against the $340,000 centre budget, preserves the flat structure and laissez-faire culture, and directly addresses the 22% labour turnover by investing in the team. Full external recruitment is rejected because it imports unknown instructors at premium wages without solving retention, and the college certificate can be sequenced so all 9 staff qualify before the peak season begins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to SWS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of SWS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SWS with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, retention and safety.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SWS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $52,000 ÷ ($22 − $9) = $52,000 ÷ $13 = 4,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $22 − $9 = $13.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $13.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SWS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 4,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 9,600 units to confirm the surf school is profitably above break-even, with a margin of safety of 5,600 units, informing whether to extend opening hours or add a second daily session.
2. Contribution per unit of $13.00 lets SWS model bundle pricing for the five-day group lesson package that 58% of surveyed visitors would book, for example a $100 five-lesson bundle would cut per-lesson contribution to $11.00, letting managers judge whether extra volume covers the $52,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $52,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the booking volumes needed to justify the $200,000 bank loan repayments and to check the new centre covers them before drawing on the further $140,000 overdraft.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($52,000 ÷ 9,600 units + $9 = $14.42 a unit) to benchmark seasonal performance, identify board-repair waste behind the 2.5-day turnaround, and decide whether to renegotiate the $9 variable cost with neoprene and foam suppliers amid the 10.6% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $13.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 9,600-unit output; five-day bundle pricing vs $52,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $340,000 centre; and unit-cost benchmarking at $14.42 to tackle repair waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SWS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SWS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.13 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $30,000 inventories + $25,000 trade receivables + $20,000 cash = $75,000; 2025 = $22,000 + $38,000 + $30,000 = $90,000. Liquidity 2024 = $75,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.25; 2025 = $90,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.50. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($75,000 − $30,000) ÷ $60,000 = $45,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.75; 2025 = ($90,000 − $22,000) ÷ $60,000 = $68,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.13.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. The 2025 liquidity figure improved from 1.25 to 1.50, meaning current assets cover current liabilities half again as much, helped by cash rising from $20,000 to $30,000 and inventories falling from $30,000 to $22,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.75 to 1.13, so SWS no longer relies on selling stock — critical while it services a $200,000 bank loan and funds a $340,000 centre with a $140,000 overdraft. However, trade receivables rose from $25,000 to $38,000, tying up cash; if hotel and booking-platform partners pay late, the stronger ratios could deteriorate quickly, and inventories fell, so wetsuit and board stock for peak weekends should be monitored.

Conclusion: SWS's financial position has improved. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.25 to 1.50, and 0.75 to 1.13) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so SWS should tighten deposit terms with hotel partners while proceeding with the learn-to-surf centre.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SWS's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SWS of installing solar showers and a board repair workshop at its new learn-to-surf centre.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Solar showers and an on-site board repair workshop reinforce SWS's eco-friendly beach image, appealing to the 58% of 450 surveyed visitors who would book a five-day package and helping win hotel referral partnerships. Lower energy bills protect the $9 variable cost per unit, and the workshop cuts the 2.5-day board-repair turnaround, keeping hire fleets available through the 84% peak-season occupancy crush.

Disadvantage: Installation and maintenance of solar equipment and workshop tooling add significant upfront cost within the $340,000 budget, and equipment faults in salt air could disrupt lessons at short notice. If the showers fail during peak weekend sessions, customer complaints — currently falling — could spike again, and the repair workshop needs a qualified technician, adding to wage costs when labour turnover is already 22%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SWS's research data, costs and centre launch.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase to $12.07 per hour, and the 10.6% rise in wetsuit neoprene and repair-foam input costs will affect SWS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): The higher base rate raises SWS's overdraft and the cost of any variable portion of its $200,000 ten-year bank loan. A 0.75% rise on a fully variable $200,000 loan adds about $1,500 a year, and it also makes consumers more cautious about discretionary spend such as lessons, though the 5.4% growth in coastal leisure spending partly offsets this. The direct effect is small and can be managed by keeping expansion costs within the fixed loan.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.07 per hour): With 24 instructor, café and hire staff, mainly seasonal and on or near minimum wage, the rise lifts every hourly wage bill. At roughly 1,200 paid hours per staff member a year, the 5.9% uplift adds roughly $17,100 a year across the team, from $11.40 to $12.07 per hour alone, which laissez-faire autonomy, productivity at 400 units per worker (9,600 units ÷ 24 staff) and the 5-day package pricing would need to absorb.

Input cost inflation (10.6% wetsuit neoprene and repair foam): SWS's $9 variable cost includes roughly $6 of materials and café inputs. An 10.6% rise on that portion adds about $0.64 per unit; at 9,600 units that is roughly $6,100 a year, squeezing contribution per unit from $13.00 toward $12.36 and raising workshop costs, though SWS can partially recover through modest price increases at peak times.

Conclusion: The 5.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Labour dominates SWS's cost base, and the rise adds roughly $17,100 a year permanently, directly eroding the margin that justifies the $340,000 centre regardless of booking volume. The 10.6% input-cost rise is the second most serious at roughly $6,100 and can be passed on or renegotiated, while the 0.75% interest-rate rise is smallest at about $1,500 and can be managed within the fixed loan; all three still require SWS to review lesson prices before the April wage change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SWS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SWS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SWS with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
